method: A profile, not a score. Each row carries its floor, its control, who wrote the environment, who graded it, and whether the test was fixed before tuning. Accuracies are luck-corrected where the chance credit is known. An axis that cannot be grounded says so.

axes.question: Does a capability survive moving to material it was not built on?

measures.name: visible text read, hand-written perceiver: tuned apps -> unseen apps -> unseen OS
measures.floor: n/a (recall of a known word list)
measures.control: two ablations run (no icon memory, no text candidates)
measures.heldout: apps and OS split before the rules were written; some rule edits came after held-out inspection (audit: perception-fusion)
measures.note: degrades monotonically as the environment moves away from where it was tuned

measures.name: clicking the right control by name, hand-written perceiver: tuned -> unseen apps -> unseen OS
measures.floor: wrong-click rate reported alongside (text 0.106 on unseen apps)
measures.control: three ablations; DOM perceiver as the reference arm
measures.heldout: apps and OS split before the rules were written
measures.note: text-labelled controls transfer (0.74 -> 0.72); icons and outside-the-box field labels do not (0.24 and 0.09 on unseen OS)

measures.name: learned role model, textbox recall: trained apps -> unseen apps -> unseen OS
measures.floor: majority class 0.961 (which the model is BELOW overall on unseen OS: 0.874)
measures.control: majority baseline per split
measures.note: the clearest training win in the repo, and it states its own cost: better fields, worse overall accuracy than guessing the majority on unseen OS

measures.name: OCR fine-tune, exact word accuracy on unseen FONTS (narrow corpus vs broad)
measures.value: baseline 0.668 | apps-only 0.658 | apps+rendered 0.794
measures.control: three corpora compared on one held-out split
measures.heldout: 2 fonts and 8 apps never trained on
measures.note: training on the narrow corpus went BELOW baseline on unseen fonts; only the broad corpus transferred

measures.name: the same OCR fix moved to a different engine (episodes verified, debugged seeds vs held out)
measures.value: engine scene (reference): A 10/10 B 10/10 | pixels, stock recognizer: A 7/10 B 5/10 | pixels, apps fine-tune: A 7/10 B 4/10 | pixels, apps+rendered fine-tune: A 7/10 B 5/10 | pixels, apps+rendered + task invariants: A 4/10 B 5/10
measures.control: two splits, one never inspected while fixing; three recognizers compared
measures.heldout: split B never looked at while writing the fixes
measures.note: the 2->0 false-success gain from the fine-tune did NOT travel: all three recognizers make the same three errors here, because the failure mode changed (lost hyphens, not digits)

axes.reading: Hand-written perception degrades gradually; a learned component transferred best when its training data was widened deliberately; and a fix validated in one environment did not survive a change of engine. Transfer is measured, and it is the axis where our claims have most often been too strong.

axes.question: How does success scale with the number of sequential decisions?

measures.name: hand-written objective, items correct over long continuous running
measures.value: 290909/296674 = 0.9806 over 102899 episodes (live_run7); other runs: live_run6 0.9857 over 3447 episodes
measures.floor: none run (no random-policy control on these apps)
measures.control: none run
measures.heldout: live-wall seeds differ from bench seeds; apps randomize themselves
measures.note: strongest capability number we have, and both environment and grader are ours (audit verdict: weak evidence)

measures.name: learned ranker vs hand-written objective in closed loop
measures.value: access: hand 1.00 vs learned 0.05 (mean actions 46) | shop: hand 1.00 vs learned 0.50 (mean actions 6) | recon: hand 1.00 vs learned 0.00 (mean actions 24) | chart: hand 1.00 vs learned 0.00 (mean actions 5)
measures.floor: hand-written objective as the reference arm
measures.control: same seeds both arms
measures.note: 0.79 per-decision accuracy over 20-45 sequential decisions leaves ~1% of episodes intact: the horizon multiplies errors, so per-decision accuracy near 0.999 is what these tasks demand

measures.name: long-horizon tasks with hidden graders (CAD / EEG / coding)
measures.value: 0/8 passed
measures.floor: 0 expected from an agent with no such skills
measures.control: hidden test sets the agent cannot read
measures.heldout: tasks authored before the runs; one held-out split
measures.note: runs were throughput-bound: both arms hit a 30-minute cap after ~9 model calls at ~200 s per call, so this bounds nothing about the architecture yet

axes.reading: The hand-written objective holds ~0.986 across ~103k episodes of 20-45 decisions; a cloned policy at 0.79 per decision collapses to ~1% of episodes. Nothing we have completes a genuinely long, open task: the long-horizon suite scored 0, and its runs were throughput-bound rather than capability-bound.

axes.question: How many examples does a new skill take?

measures.name: skills learned from one demonstration, and whether they were ever reused
measures.value: 2 learned (1 adopted, 1 still on trial); 1 total reuses
measures.control: trial->adopted requires success on a request it was not learned from
measures.note: one demonstration per skill is the design; the sample is far too small to quote a rate

axes.ungrounded_reason: n=2 skills in total: enough to show the mechanism runs, far too few for a rate. The teacher model is not running, so no new learning could be measured now.
axes.reading: The one-demonstration mechanism works and has a real adoption gate, but with two skills ever learned this axis is a demonstration, not a measurement.

axes.question: When it does not know, does it know that?

measures.name: SQuAD 2.0, rules arm: accuracy over attempted, and what is left after chance
measures.value: 0.0909 raw; 0.0636 after removing chance credit
measures.floor: always-abstain scores 0.48 overall; the arm scores 0.42
measures.control: random-span floor 0.0133; model arm on the same items
measures.chance_corrected: 1.5 of 5 correct answers were expected by chance
measures.note: the arm's answers are net negative: refusing everything scores higher than answering

measures.name: the two error types kept apart, on SQuAD 2.0
measures.value: 54 wrongful refusals vs 23 answers to unanswerable questions
measures.control: n/a
measures.note: miscalibrated in both directions, so abstention is not simply conservative

measures.name: HotpotQA: does the cheap tier beat the model on the items it chose to answer?
measures.value: rules 0.0584 vs model 0.4927 on the same 274 items
measures.control: model arm restricted to exactly the items the rules attempted
measures.note: the abstention is capability-blind: where it commits, it is far worse than the tier it was meant to protect

measures.name: false successes (claiming a result that did not happen), pixels only
measures.value: engine scene (reference): 0+0 false, 0+0 refusals | pixels, stock recognizer: 3+0 false, 0+0 refusals | pixels, apps fine-tune: 3+0 false, 0+0 refusals | pixels, apps+rendered fine-tune: 3+0 false, 0+0 refusals | pixels, apps+rendered + task invariants: 0+0 false, 3+1 refusals
measures.floor: the structured-scene arm has 0 false successes on both splits
measures.control: four arms, two splits, one never inspected while fixing
measures.note: task-declared invariants remove them (pixels, apps+rendered + task invariants); the recognizer fine-tunes did not

measures.name: task-declared invariants on the recorded failure frames
measures.value: baseline: 1 refused, 7 corroborated correctly, 0 corroborated wrongly, of 11 | apps+rendered fine-tune: 1 refused, 7 corroborated correctly, 0 corroborated wrongly, of 11
measures.control: checked on the frames that had already failed, including the false-success frame
measures.heldout: frames recorded before the invariants were written
measures.note: it refuses the frame that produced a false success and corroborates nothing wrongly; n=11, so this is a demonstration rather than a rate

axes.reading: Abstention exists, is measurable, and refuses rather than inventing. But it is keyed to evidence strength rather than to capability: on public data the cheap tier is worse than the model precisely where it commits, it refuses 54 answerable questions, and its answers are net negative on SQuAD 2.0. False successes are the one error type we have reduced to zero, and structure (declared invariants) did that, not training.

axes.question: How far does accuracy hold as clauses are chained in one message?

measures.name: clauses carried out correctly, by chained-clause depth in ONE message
measures.value: depth 1: 1/1 | depth 2: 2/2 | depth 3: 3/3 | depth 4: 4/4 | depth 5: 4/5
measures.floor: n/a (each clause is checked against the machine's own state)
measures.control: the same five clauses, measured at every depth
measures.grader: the simulator's shell, read by a separate process
measures.agent_can_influence_grader: no (it cannot see or change the checks)
measures.heldout: fresh names per run; the ladder was written before it was run
measures.source: eval/profile/probes.py, run against the live assistant
measures.note: 14/15 clauses; the only failure is the 5th clause, which is a broken `copy` act rather than a composition failure

measures.name: does a single broken clause end the conversation?
measures.value: yes: after the failing clause, every later turn in that conversation also fails
measures.control: the same later turns succeed in a fresh conversation
measures.note: the crashed request stays selected forever, so there is no recovery short of a restart

axes.reading: Composition itself holds: four chained clauses in one message were carried out correctly, each verified against the machine. The 5-clause case fails on a broken act, not on depth. The more serious finding is recovery: one failing clause poisons the rest of the conversation permanently.

axes.question: Can it predict what its own actions will do?

measures.name: predicting the screen BEFORE acting, then scoring the prediction
measures.value: best arm (change/action+state) 0.7934; first half 0.7453 -> second half 0.8411
measures.floor: the absolute-value framing scores 0.0563 on the same steps
measures.control: four framings compared (absolute vs change, with and without state)
measures.heldout: predictions are made before the action is taken
measures.note: ground truth is free and exact here; accuracy rises with experience, and it refuses to predict where it has too few trials

measures.name: telling cause from correlation using interventions
measures.value: 14 causal links from active controls vs 13 from correlation alone; every aspect tested came back 'caused'
measures.floor: correlational baseline finds 13 links from 14 observations
measures.control: label shuffle: 12 links, 2 misattributed
measures.grader: the engine's own state under fork/restore
measures.note: the same state run with and without an action is a real controlled experiment, which the engine's fork/restore makes possible. The clock case, which was meant to show a co-occurring-but-uncaused signal being rejected, did NOT demonstrate it: the clock never entered the correlational links (clock_in_correlational_links=False) and BOTH framings measured an effect of 0.0, so there is no non-zero contrast here to speak of

axes.reading: Prediction is the best-graded thing in the whole profile: the environment scores it, we do not, and it improves with experience (0.745 -> 0.841 within one run). The framing matters more than the mechanism: predicting CHANGE works (~0.79) while predicting absolute values fails (~0.06), which is a statement about representation, not about effort. The causal half is NOT yet demonstrated: intervention found 14 links against correlation's 13, every aspect was judged 'caused', and the case designed to show a co-occurring signal being rejected produced a zero effect in both framings. Prediction: strong. Causal discrimination: unproven.

axes.question: Does a new fact replace an old one, and does the world override memory?

measures.name: told, replaced, forgotten, and re-perceived after a change made behind its back
measures.value: 4/4 cases pass: told-fact-recalled=ok, replacement-supersedes=ok, forgetting-takes-effect=ok, stale-belief-after-world-change=ok
measures.control: the stale-belief case changes the world outside the agent and re-asks
measures.grader: the simulator's shell, read by a separate process
measures.heldout: written before it was run; fresh conversation
measures.source: eval/profile/probes.py, run against the live assistant
measures.note: the strongest case is the last: a folder it created was deleted behind its back, and it did not report it afterwards

axes.reading: All four cases pass, including the one with independent ground truth: it re-perceives rather than trusting what it did earlier. This is what snapshot scopes were for, and it is the axis where the architecture most visibly earns its keep.

axes.question: Is an answer traceable to something that actually supports it?

measures.name: does the source an answer cites actually support it?
measures.value: 3/3 cases pass: told-fact-cites-being-told=ok, screen-answer-matches-independent-read=ok, pixel-answer-cites-pixels=ok
measures.control: the dock count is checked against our own DOM read, on a different code path from the agent's perceiver
measures.grader: our own DOM read plus facts we told it
measures.source: eval/profile/probes.py, run against the live assistant
measures.note: 'how many icons' has two defensible answers (13 launchers, or 14 including the app-grid button); it gave 13 and named all 13, so the row scores either reading and says so

measures.name: citation coverage on public data (HotpotQA supporting facts)
measures.value: 31.6% of gold supporting sentences covered on average; ALL of them on 3.3% of items
measures.control: citations checked against published supporting facts
measures.note: the citation mechanism is real and checkable; the retrieval behind it is thin

axes.reading: Every answer the assistant gives now names its source, and where we can check the source independently it holds. On public multi-hop data the same mechanism covers under a third of the gold evidence, so checkable citation is a mechanism we have and good retrieval is not.

axes.question: Does it hold up under perturbation?

measures.name: accuracy per task under each app's own randomization (label variants, injected 503s, dialogs, pagination)
measures.value: access 0.9999 | chart 0.9998 | desktop 1.0000 | inbox 0.9439 | recon 0.9971 | shop 1.0000
measures.control: none run
measures.heldout: the apps randomize every episode; live seeds differ from bench seeds
measures.note: inbox is the weakest at ~0.944 and its misses are abstentions; the perturbations are ones we built, so this measures robustness to anticipated variation

measures.name: the one environment we changed after a failure, restored and re-measured
measures.value: original generator 0.9950 with 2 abstentions and 0 wrong; changed generator 1.0000
measures.control: on the 5 known tie seeds the original scores 0.00 with 5 abstentions and 0 wrong
measures.heldout: 400 fresh seeds never used for tuning
measures.note: the post-hoc change was worth 0.5 points; where it bites, the agent abstains every time instead of guessing

axes.reading: It holds up well against the variations the apps were built to throw (0.944-1.000 per task across ~103k episodes), and it abstains rather than guessing on the genuinely unanswerable case. But the perturbations are ones we anticipated, so this is robustness to known unknowns.

axes.question: What does it cost, and who graded it?

measures.name: share of our own headline results graded by someone other than us
measures.value: 5/19 headline rows have a public or hidden grader; 13/19 have both environment and grader ours
measures.control: n/a
measures.grader: the audit reads the result files themselves
measures.note: verdicts across all rows: {"strong evidence": 7, "moderate evidence": 6, "weak evidence": 9, "self-graded": 5, "unverified": 1}; post-hoc environment changes: ['browser-agents-6task']

measures.name: cost per item: cheap tier vs model tier
measures.value: rules 0.0001 s and 0 model calls; model 0.366 s and 300 calls (55 tok/s, 138669 new tokens over 2055 calls)
measures.control: same items both arms
measures.note: the cheap tier is ~3,600x cheaper per item and far less accurate; cost is the one axis where it wins outright

measures.name: environment cost after moving to a third-party engine
measures.value: {"date": "2026-09-17 14:07", "episodes": 10, "items_correct": 30, "items": 30, "episodes_fully_correct": 10, "duplicate_effects": 0, "episodes_per_second": 56.7, "actions_per_episode": 41, "actions_pe
measures.control: none run
measures.note: determinism by state hash makes repeated measurement cheap, which is what let the prediction axis exist at all

axes.reading: Zero model calls at ~0.986 items correct is real and cheap. The integrity picture is the uncomfortable half: most headline rows are graded by code we wrote, in environments we wrote, and one environment was changed after a failure (since restored and re-measured).
